qt: to the Council Marc Jongen (ESN) Subject:

On the morning of 3 January, Berlin’s power grid was rocked by an arson attack that left 45 000 households and 2000 businesses without electricity for days and depriving many people of heating and adequate medical care. An 83-year-old woman died, probably as a result of this terrorist act.1 The so-called Vulkangruppe (Volcano Group), which had already attracted attention for violent attacks against such targets as the Tesla factory in Grünheide near Berlin, has claimed responsibility and is considered by German security authorities to be on the leftwing extremist spectrum.2 The group openly espouses an environmentally extremist and radical feminist agenda, as well as an affinity with Antifa ideology. 1.
What connections between the Vulkangruppe and other groups and individuals on the extreme-left or Antifa spectrum are known to the Council by name?

What specific measures (e.g. travel bans, freezing of assets, criminalisation of the recruitment of new members) does the Council plan to take against the Vulkangruppe, its members and, where applicable, organisations and individuals associated with it?
What further measures does the Council plan to take to protect the public and critical infrastructure from left-wing extremist terrorist attacks such as the one in Berlin?
at: The information requested by the Honourable Member is not available to the Council. On a general note, decisions to adopt restrictive measures against individuals or entities (sanctions including asset freezes and travel bans) are taken by the Council of the European Union, based on proposals from the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy or a Member State. The proposed measures are politically agreed upon by the Committee of Permanent Representatives (Coreper) and then adopted by the Council. These measures enter into force upon publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. Regarding restrictive measures, the Council does not disclose the discussions or reasons behind a decision before it is made. Furthermore, restrictive measures are not punitive but rather seek to bring about a change in the policy or conduct of those targeted, with a view to promoting the objectives of the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy. They are therefore not construed as sanctions aimed at criminalising specific individuals or behaviour. The Council regularly discusses threats to EU critical infrastructure, including with regard to the provision of essential services in the energy sector, with the objective of supporting close cooperation among Member States to strengthen resilience. A Council recommendation on an EU-wide coordinated approach to strengthen the resilience of critical infrastructure and a Council recommendation on a blueprint to coordinate a response at EU level to disruptions to critical infrastructure with significant cross-border relevance were adopted in December 2022 and June 2024, respectively. These acts complement the Directive on the resilience of critical entities (CER Directive) adopted in December 2022.
